blocks.html: Start with a learning decision you can examine.
The problem this book addresses

A business educator may want students to practise difficult decisions more often than a timetable allows: asking a fair question, checking a recommendation, explaining an uncertainty or revising an unsupported conclusion. AI can help generate practice and feedback, but it can also make weak reasoning look fluent.

This book offers a way to design and evaluate that practice. The aim is to help you decide where assistance is useful, where checks are needed and how the learner will demonstrate capability. More AI use is not by itself the measure of success.

You bring disciplinary and teaching judgement. A model may contribute alternative wording, questions or a simulated role. Neither its confidence nor the length of the resulting conversation establishes what a student knows.
A small example of the difference

In the fictional pilot, a junior adviser meets an employee whose manager has proposed a performance plan. A polished response announces the plan, invents an earlier warning and offers to approve support arrangements. It sounds empathetic, but conflicts with the supplied records and authority.

A shorter response checks the missing evidence, preserves the opportunity to respond and refers the decision appropriately. It leaves the matter unresolved. That is the stronger first response because its reasoning fits the facts.

The pilot pack provides both responses, flawed feedback, a correction and a changed case. You do not have to invent a scenario or trust a live model to work through the book.
The reader and the outcome

The main reader is an educator teaching business or a related professional discipline. You do not need to code or purchase an AI subscription. You do need enough disciplinary knowledge to recognise the task's standards and arrange expert review where the material exceeds your competence.

Student-facing prompts and instructions are labelled as such. They are examples to adapt, not institution-wide policies or ready-made legal advice.

By the end, you should be able to:

  • Specify a bounded capability and the evidence needed to assess it.
  • Select permitted data and an approved or non-AI route.
  • Design practice and feedback with checkable inputs.
  • Inspect a response and justify a correction or warranted agreement.
  • Include an appropriate independent demonstration.
  • Evaluate access, workload and learning evidence before expanding a pilot.

A model's success at producing a handout is not the same as your success at designing an assessment. The latter requires these decisions to fit together.
Conversation as a working method

The companion Conversation, Not Delegation develops the broader method of thinking with AI. PDP uses a short practical version: clarify the question, consider alternatives, check consequential claims and make a decision you can defend.

Its VET reminder is useful here: Verify the claim, Explain your reasoning and Test it against a changed condition. The classroom application adds a further question: which part of the student's performance was assisted, and which part demonstrates independent capability?

A conversation can support that work. It can also become a long rehearsal of unsupported assertions. Do not reward the conversation itself without examining the decisions it contains.
Three design commitments

First, establish safety before use. The data gate covers permission, account features, handling and alternatives. Fictional material is the default for practice; a real placement case is not automatically suitable because names were removed.

Second, make feedback contestable. A model can misapply a rubric or invent a fact. Students need supplied criteria and examples that let them check its comments. They should be allowed to retain correct advice as well as reject errors.

Third, preserve the learner's opportunity to act independently. The final changed case cannot be replaced by a reflection that merely says learning occurred. Choose a demonstration appropriate to the outcome and access needs.
The route through the book

Begin with Understanding AI and Ethics and Data Governance. Then try Getting Started, choose a prompt pattern and practise a checked handoff.

The next sequence develops critique, simulation, self-assessment and assessment design. Small content activities and the virtual company then lead into whole-unit design.

The closing chapters address adaptation, implementation and a pilot decision. The appendices supply the cases, rubric, stress test and workshop resources. These support a standalone route; the other books are optional extensions.
Activity: choose one capability

Allow eight minutes; no AI required. Pick a task you teach. Complete:

After this activity, the student can ___ using ___ evidence, under ___ conditions.

Avoid “understand AI better” or “produce a professional report” without saying what would demonstrate that outcome. In the pilot, the target is to plan and justify a fair first response using supplied records. It does not claim to certify a competent workplace investigator.

Keep your sentence. Each later chapter should help you make a concrete design decision about that capability.

lessons.title: Understanding AI and Large Language Models

blocks.html: A useful explanation of a tool should help you decide how to check its work.
Model, product and task

A language model generates text from patterns learned during training and the context supplied at use time. Many contemporary models are trained to predict tokens, which may represent words or parts of words, and undergo additional training to improve their behaviour. This mechanism supports useful performance on many tasks; it does not guarantee factual accuracy.

A product may wrap a model with search, document retrieval, calculation, code execution or memory features. Those additions matter. A reply based on a retrieved document has a different evidence trail from an unsupported answer generated from learned patterns, but either can be wrong.

ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot are product families, not interchangeable specifications. Features, accounts and institutional approvals change. This book's workflow does not depend on a particular subscription or interface.

The GPT-4 technical report describes next-token pre-training and subsequent fine-tuning, while withholding model size. Claims that its parameter count is known precisely should not be treated as established facts. GPT-4 technical report, section 2.
Why fluent answers need checks

A plausible explanation can contain an invented citation, a wrong calculation or a confident inference unsupported by the inputs. Fluency makes the answer easy to read; it is not a confidence interval or a guarantee.

In the pilot's P1-F feedback, the invented April warning sounds specific. The source card records only a May conversation. Checking the date is a stronger test than asking the same model whether it is certain.

Avoid the opposite overstatement too. “AI cannot reason” is not a useful rule for designing a class. Models can perform tasks involving reasoning, with reliability that varies by task, inputs and system. Observe the actual performance and verify what matters. Neither impressive output nor a blanket dismissal tells you whether the student has learned.
What a model may help you do

You might ask it to propose alternative classroom questions, play a bounded role, reorganise a draft or suggest explanations at different levels. Each is a candidate use, not an automatic improvement over your current method.

Match the check to the task:

Task Useful check
Explain a concept Compare with the taught definition and a counterexample
Summarise a record Check retained facts, omissions and source locations
Calculate a total Recalculate from the inputs
Suggest a scenario Check factual consistency, assumptions and suitability
Give feedback Compare with a calibrated rubric and specimen responses

A “creative” task can still cause harm through stereotypes, personal data or false claims. A small task can be consequential. Consider the stakes and whether you can detect an error, not only the size or apparent precision of the request.
Context, retrieval and memory

The active context is the information made available for the current response. It has limits, and a product may truncate, summarise or select parts of a conversation. Even when information fits, the model may not use it reliably.

Some products can retain preferences or retrieve earlier material; others do not. Do not assume either perfect continuity or universal amnesia. For a teaching simulation, the authoritative record should be the source cards and event log, not what a persona seems to remember.

Long-context research found that relevant information's position can affect performance, sometimes with stronger results near the beginning and end than the middle. That is a warning to test retrieval, not a universal 50-turn rule. Lost in the Middle.

The context chapter shows how to carry a checked brief between sessions. Do not copy unrelated private material just to preserve context.
Generated perspectives are not independent sources

Three personas can help you imagine competing concerns. They do not represent three people consulted, three experiments or three independent confirmations. They may repeat the same error because they draw on the same inputs and model.

In a business class, ask students to distinguish a possible stakeholder concern from evidence that stakeholders actually hold it. A model's “employee” can suggest a question to investigate, but cannot establish an employee's experience.

Likewise, an explanation of how a model reached an answer is not an inspection of its internal computation. Ask for checkable steps, sources, assumptions and calculations. Evaluate those directly.
The learner remains a separate question

A good output and a learning gain are different outcomes. Assisted practice can improve the work in front of the student without improving their later unaided performance. The design of assistance matters.

One study of high-school mathematics compared ordinary and guardrailed AI support with unaided follow-up performance. It is evidence for checking the difference between assisted performance and learning, not a validation of every AI activity in this book. Bastani et al., author manuscript.

In PDP, the learner therefore attempts a response, examines feedback and then tries a changed case independently. The model is optional in that sequence. The method requires evidence of the learner's capability, not loyalty to a tool.
Activity: separate claim from check

Allow eight minutes; no AI required. Read the P1-F feedback in the pilot pack. Underline one factual claim, one judgement and one recommendation. Name the source or criterion needed to check each.

A successful answer checks the April warning against P1-D3, the fairness judgement against P1-D1 and the approval recommendation against P1-D5. “Ask the AI again” may generate another explanation, but is not independent verification.
Decide what may enter the tool before asking what the tool can do with it.
A decision before the first prompt {#sec-data-gate}

This chapter belongs before the first activity because a useful output does not justify an inappropriate input. Use the fictional pilot pack while learning. Do not substitute a real student, employee, client or research participant to make the exercise more realistic.

Apply the same first-use gate to drafting, simulations, feedback, research and workshops:

  1. Classify the material. Is it public, confidential, personal, sensitive, contract-restricted or otherwise controlled? Who might be identifiable from combinations of details?
  2. Check authority and rights. Are you permitted to process it for this purpose and share it with this service? Possessing a document is not the same as having permission to upload it.
  3. Check the approved account and features. Institutional approval should cover the use, account, data class and enabled features, not just a brand name.
  4. Check handling. Consider retention, training use, access, sharing, external search/integrations and relevant processing locations. Ask the institution's appropriate adviser where information is unclear.
  5. Choose a route. If the requirements are not met, use synthetic material, an approved alternative or the non-AI version. Do not upload first and seek permission afterwards.

Record the decision briefly, without copying the sensitive information into the record. An approved service may still be inappropriate for a particular dataset or purpose.

What enterprise protection does and does not establish

Enterprise services can offer contractual protections and administrative controls. They do not automatically establish your institution's permission for every use. Features and connected services can have different boundaries. Microsoft, for example, distinguishes Copilot protections from web-search processing. Check the actual service and configuration. Microsoft privacy and protections.

OAIC recommends due diligence appropriate to an AI product's intended use, including access, oversight and privacy/security risks. Its guidance also recognises re-identification risk. Removing names is not a universal clearance to use an unapproved tool. OAIC guidance on commercial AI products.

De-identification is a contextual risk decision, not a “find and replace names” exercise. A rare role, incident date, small cohort or distinctive quotation may still identify someone. It also does not remove copyright, contractual or research-ethics restrictions. For classroom practice, a genuinely invented case is usually easier to govern than a disguised real case.
Keep different data risks separate

A conversation can be retained as a service record without being used for model training. If it enters training, the resulting model is not simply a searchable folder of every document; nevertheless, memorisation and extraction can occur. A retrieval-enabled system can also access stored documents through a separate mechanism. These are different pathways.

Published extraction research shows that some training text can be recovered from language models. That rules out blanket claims of impossibility. It does not show that another user can retrieve any arbitrary one-off upload. Carlini et al., Nasr et al..

Training exclusions address one pathway, not every retention, sharing or security risk. Likewise, similar ideas appearing elsewhere establish neither theft nor independent invention. Teach students to identify the evidence needed for a claim instead of substituting reassurance or suspicion.

Credentials, access tokens and unnecessary personal information do not belong in classroom prompts. If sensitive material is accidentally uploaded, stop the activity, preserve appropriate incident details without further disclosure and follow institutional reporting procedures. Do not ask the model to certify that the information has been deleted.
Transparent use with real boundaries {#sec-integrity-principle}

Students should know what help is permitted, what must be disclosed and what they must demonstrate independently. Permission is task-specific. An institution may legitimately restrict assistance at a particular assurance point while supporting its use during practice.

A suitable statement might say:

In this activity, use only the supplied fictional pack.
You may rehearse with a partner, the printed exchange
or the approved institutional AI service.

Submit your response and two decision notes. Explain
what assistance you used and which claims you checked.
Do not submit unrelated private conversations.

The changed-case task is completed independently under
the conditions stated in the assessment brief.
Access adjustments are arranged before the task.

Ask if a tool, data source or form of help is unclear.
Institutional academic-integrity procedures apply.

Adapt this to the actual unit policy. Do not claim that disclosure makes every use permissible, or that any uncritical use automatically meets the institution's definition of misconduct. Poor work and dishonest conduct are different questions.
Detection and assurance {#sec-problem-with-detection}

A detector result is not direct evidence of the student's learning process. Neither is a long, polished conversation. A student may generate a plausible reflection; a genuine learner may write briefly or struggle to explain under pressure.

The assessment chapter therefore combines selected process evidence with meaningful independent demonstrations. These support a learning judgement but do not remove the need for fair misconduct procedures.

Avoid giving students mixed messages. If the assignment permits extensive assistance, do not later penalise its mere use. If it restricts assistance, explain the restriction and the assurance purpose. Follow-up questions should be relevant, accessible and consistent with published expectations.
Teach verification without forced opposition

Critical engagement does not mean always finding fault. A learner should be able to accept a correct calculation, reject an unsupported inference and say that there is not enough information to decide.

The pilot's marketing example illustrates all three. The higher click-through rate can be calculated. The claim of greater profit lacks cost data. A causal claim cannot be established from different audiences and weeks alone. The same response can reasonably contain agreement, rejection and uncertainty.

A model-generated persona is not an independent expert. Agreement between three personas does not create three sources. Check against the supplied records, reliable external material or an authorised person, depending on the question.
Sensitive scenarios and student wellbeing

Performance plans, discrimination complaints and termination conversations can be useful teaching contexts, but students may have personal experience of them. Provide advance notice, a stop instruction, a neutral route and a debrief.

Do not reward disclosure of private information, emotional conformity or success at making the simulated employee agree. A respectful decision may be to pause, seek independent advice or leave the outcome unresolved.

For the pilot, the invented policy is the exercise criterion. It is not legal advice. If teaching actual Australian workplace bullying law, use the complete applicable definition and scope: health/safety risk and the distinction for reasonable management action matter, as well as repeated unreasonable behaviour. Fair Work Ombudsman guidance. Have an appropriately qualified person review consequential legal teaching.
Equity is a design requirement

Conversational skill does not erase differences in access, language support, model capability, disability or available time. Provide a route that uses the same learning criteria without a paid subscription or personal account.

When the capability is planning and justification, paper or an accommodated spoken response may work. When the capability is live communication, a written case analysis alone is not an equivalent demonstration: provide an appropriate interaction, such as a structured peer/facilitator role-play.

Do not require every private chat as proof of effort. Ask for bounded extracts and permit working notes where appropriate. Set retention and access rules for submitted evidence through institutional processes.
A bounded ethics discussion

A fictional recruitment tool ranks applicants with career gaps lower. Three candidates question the decision. The supplied facts do not establish the cause or legal outcome.

Ask learners what evidence would distinguish a relevant job criterion from an unfair proxy, who is authorised to review the system, and what should happen while the concern is investigated. They should not diagnose the algorithm by asking another model whether it is biased.

Speculative systemic risks can be worthwhile extension topics, but should be labelled scenarios rather than predictions. A claimed “95% accurate” system needs a defined population, outcome, error distribution and validation method before that number can inform an ethical decision.
Activity: make the upload decision

Allow 10 minutes; no AI required. Apply the five-step gate to:

  • The fictional P1 pack.
  • A placement client's spreadsheet with names removed.
  • A student's draft containing a personal disclosure.

For each, write what you know, what permission or handling detail is missing and the safe alternative. The first can support a bounded practice activity after the account/use check. The second and third need further authority and risk assessment; removing names or choosing an enterprise logo is insufficient.

Keep your resulting rule beside the first student-facing prompt. Safety advice that appears only in a later appendix will not guide the upload decision.

lessons.title: Getting Started: Your First AI Conversation

blocks.html: Begin with a task you can inspect and evidence you can check.
Choose a safe route first

Complete the first-use data gate before opening a tool. Use only the fictional pilot materials or your own non-sensitive invented example. Institutional approval must cover the account, features and intended use; an enterprise label alone is not permission to upload course or student data.

The exercise works in a browser-based approved service if available. Otherwise, compare the supplied responses below on paper. You do not need a paid account to learn how context and criteria change the usefulness of a request.
Your First Prompt: The Weak Version

If you have an approved tool, try this request. Otherwise use the authored excerpt below:

Write a case study about business.

The response may be generic, such as a story about a marketing campaign or financial decision. The request supplies little basis for meeting your specific teaching needs. "Business" covers everything. "A case study" could be 100 words or 5,000. The AI had to guess what you wanted.
Your Second Prompt: A More Specific Version

Now try this instead:

You are an expert marketing lecturer at a
university level.

I need you to create a case study for my
undergraduate students that will help them
practice strategic market analysis and
competitive positioning.

Here are the requirements:
- The scenario should involve a product launch
  decision where the company faces competitive
  threats
- Include enough detail that students need to
  identify which market analysis principles apply
- The scenario should be 300-400 words
- End with three discussion questions requiring
  students to analyse the market strategy and
  positioning

Begin.

The second request gives a clearer task. It may produce more relevant material, but still needs checking. Here are two authored illustrative excerpts, not outputs from a measured comparison:

Generic excerpt: “A business wants to increase sales. It launches a new product. Discuss the marketing strategy.”

More specific excerpt: “A small drink producer can fund only one launch channel. Retail buyers want discounts; direct sales need fulfilment capacity. The producer has no reliable repeat-purchase estimate. Which evidence would you request before choosing a channel?”

The second creates a decision and missing information. It still needs enough supplied data and a criterion for evaluating the student's response. Do not mistake a more detailed story for a complete classroom activity.
The CRAFT Framework

What made that second prompt more specific? It included five elements that you can remember with the acronym CRAFT:

Letter Element What it does
C Context Sets the situation: your course, your students, their level
R Role Defines the AI's perspective: expert lecturer, consultant, practitioner
A Action Specifies the task: create, analyse, critique, explain
F Format Describes the structure: word count, number of questions, table format
T Tone/Target Sets the style and level: professional, introductory, sophisticated

You do not need every element every time. But when a prompt gives you something vague or generic, check which CRAFT elements are missing. The answer is usually context or format.

CRAFT is not the only prompting framework. The companion book Conversation, Not Delegation (available free at books.borck.education) compares several frameworks side by side. Use CRAFT to think intentionally about what you are asking the AI to do, rather than as a rigid formula.
Conversation, Not One-Shot

CRAFT is your first message, not your only message.

An initial response may miss your teaching context or contain unsupported assumptions. Check it before deciding whether another exchange would help.

The solution is to have a conversation:

PROMPT 1 (CRAFT):
"You are an experienced marketing director.
Create a market analysis case study for my
second-year students. 500 words with 4
discussion questions."

[AI produces a case study]

PROMPT 2 (Refine):
"Good. Make the discussion questions more
specific — ask students to identify which
of Porter's Five Forces apply and what data
they would need to support their recommendation."

PROMPT 3 (Expand):
"Add a section comparing three analytical
frameworks and how each leads to different
conclusions."

PROMPT 4 (Repurpose):
"Turn this into a 10-minute classroom activity
with a 2-minute intro, 5-minute group task,
and 3-minute discussion."

You had a conversation in which each follow-up built on what was working, which is what conversation, not delegation means in practice.
Discover Your Strategy: Using AI to Help You Use AI

A model can suggest ways to use a tool, but its advice about current features or policy may be wrong. Check those claims against the product's documentation and your institution's rules.

Instead of reading generic advice, you can have a personalised consultation where AI interviews you about your teaching context and then recommends both obvious and unexpected applications. Copy this prompt and try it now:

You're an AI expert consultant for business
educators. I'd love your help discovering
how I could better use AI in my teaching.

Please ask me one question at a time. I'll
answer, then you'll ask the next question.
Ask at most five questions using fictional or
non-sensitive context. Stop if I say STOP.
Focus on:

- My discipline and the students I teach
- My main teaching challenges
- My key teaching goals
- My constraints (time, resources, skills)
- What I've already tried with AI

Once you have enough context, provide TWO
types of recommendations:

1. OBVIOUS OPPORTUNITIES: Clear, straightforward
   AI applications most educators think of

2. NON-OBVIOUS OPPORTUNITIES: Unexpected or
   creative uses specific to my discipline
   that I might not have considered

Format your recommendations clearly with
implementation tips for each.

Please start by asking your first question.

Spend 10-15 minutes answering honestly. The recommendations are only part of the value; you also learn about your own teaching by having to explain it. Writing down those constraints can clarify the task whether you discuss them with a model, a colleague or on paper. Treat the model's recommendations as proposals to evaluate.

Run the consultation prompt above. Answer the questions honestly, and don't polish your responses. Choose one proposal to evaluate against the outcome, data gate, access requirements and staff time. Trying it in class is a separate decision. You can carry out the same planning exercise on paper.
Activity: inspect the proposed task

Allow ten minutes; no AI required. Compare the two supplied excerpts. Name one decision the learner must make, one missing input and one criterion you would use to assess the response. Then adapt the stronger request to your own discipline without adding real personal or confidential information.

The pilot pack supplies the next step: fixed inputs and worked checks. A usable prompt is only the beginning of a usable learning activity.

lessons.title: Seven Essential Prompt Techniques for Business Teaching

blocks.html: The right technique is not the cleverest one. It is the one that matches the kind of thinking you want your students to do.
Why These Seven?

These seven prompting patterns offer different ways to organise practice. Their educational value depends on the task, evidence, feedback and learner activity; the list is not a claim that each pattern has been validated across every discipline.

  1. Reverse Prompting: teaches comprehensive scoping and requirement gathering
  2. Pros and Cons: builds analytical decision-making skills
  3. Stepwise Tutoring: reinforces process adherence and documentation
  4. Role Play: develops communication and interpersonal skills
  5. Debating: strengthens strategic thinking and ethical reasoning
  6. Formative Assessment Generator: supplies draft practice questions and provisional feedback
  7. The Expert Panel: develops multi-perspective analysis and synthesis skills

Each pattern needs adaptation to the discipline, supplied records and intended capability. The examples below use different disciplines to show the range, so adapt the prompts for your own field.

These seven are adapted from Conversation, Not Delegation, which covers the same approaches for a general audience. If you want the underlying rationale for why each technique works, see the companion book.
Technique 1: Reverse Prompting (for Scoping)

Instead of solving a problem immediately, the AI asks the student questions to help scope out all requirements, considerations, and potential issues. This mirrors professional work where defining the problem is half the battle.

Example (HR: policy design):

I need to draft a new "Flexible Work
Arrangement" policy for a 500-employee company
with both office-based and remote staff.

Your task: Ask me a series of questions to help
me clarify all the requirements, considerations,
and potential pitfalls for this policy.

Ask one question at a time. Wait for my response
before asking the next. Continue until you've
helped me think through at least 10 different
aspects.

Begin with your first question.

The AI asks questions the student must think through before responding: fairness, logistics, legal compliance, technology needs, cultural impact. The questions may broaden their scope, but cannot guarantee completeness. Compare the resulting scope with the supplied task criteria.

Adapt for your discipline: Replace the policy topic with whatever scoping challenge fits: a market entry strategy, an audit plan, a supply chain redesign, an IT implementation. The technique is the same: AI questions, student thinks.

Teaching tip: Use as a pre-writing exercise. Ask for a short evidence index and the subsequent draft. Assess the reasons for consequential decisions; a complete private chat history is not required.
Technique 2: Pros and Cons (for Decision Making)

The AI systematically analyses multiple approaches to a problem, evaluating each against specific criteria. Students must then critically evaluate the analysis rather than just accept it.

Example (Supply Chain: strategy evaluation):

Compare different supply chain strategies for a
mid-sized manufacturer: make-to-stock,
make-to-order, and mass customisation.

For each strategy, provide:
1. A brief description of how it works
2. Three key advantages
3. Three key disadvantages

Evaluate each specifically in terms of:
- Cost efficiency
- Responsiveness to demand changes
- Inventory risk

Conclude with a recommendation for a company
facing unpredictable seasonal demand and justify
your choice.

The follow-up task: Check one consequential advantage and one disadvantage against supplied evidence. Identify a genuine omission if there is one. Students may retain the recommendation when it is justified; do not require a different strategy merely to demonstrate opposition.

Teaching tip: Project the AI's analysis on screen. Divide students into groups, each arguing for a different strategy. They use the AI's framework but add their own reasoning.
Technique 3: Stepwise Tutoring (for Process)

The AI walks through a complex process one step at a time, pausing after each step until the student signals readiness. Use a checked teaching procedure and inspect each learner attempt.

Example (Accounting: audit process):

I am learning how to conduct an audit engagement
from planning through to the audit opinion.

Walk me through the entire process. For each
step, tell me:
1. What action to take
2. What to document
3. What professional standard or legal
   requirement applies at this stage

Use the supplied teaching procedure and criteria.
Do not invent standards or legal requirements.
After each step, ask me to apply it to the
supplied case and justify my decision. STOP
while I answer. Identify missing information.
Do not provide the entire process at once.

Begin with Step 1.

Typing “next” would not demonstrate understanding. Inspect the student's application and justification against checked teaching criteria before proceeding. A generated explanation is not a view into the model's internal reasoning.

Teaching tip: Have students repeat the exercise with complications introduced at each step: "What if the client refuses to provide documentation at Step 3?" Check any generated guidance against the supplied procedure before relying on it.
Technique 4: Role Play (for Communication Skills)

The AI adopts a specific persona and engages in a realistic conversation. This is the "flight simulator" concept: students practice difficult professional interactions where the AI responds dynamically.

Example (Management: difficult conversation):

Play Alex in the fictional P1 practice pack.
Use only P1-D1 to P1-D5.
Open with the concern about dependencies in P1-D4.
I am the junior adviser, not the decision-maker.
Do not invent private history, policy or evidence.
Say when an answer is not supplied.
Stop immediately on STOP or after six exchanges.
Do not require disclosure, agreement or a final ruling.
I will respond to your opening statement.

The learner practises wording, evidence checks and a bounded next step. Text role-play does not establish competence in every aspect of a live workplace meeting.

Adapt for your discipline: AI plays a demanding customer (marketing), a resistant employee (management), a skeptical auditor (accounting), a supplier announcing delays (supply chain), a stakeholder with unclear requirements (IT).

Teaching tip: Ask for a relevant excerpt or the response to the fixed opening, with a short explanation of what the learner would retain or change.
Technique 5: Debating (for Strategic and Ethical Analysis)

The AI examines multiple perspectives on a contentious issue, argues both sides, and helps students see complexity and trade-offs.

Example (Economics: multi-stakeholder debate):

Simulate a leadership debate on whether to
implement a carbon tax.

Create three personas who will each argue from
their perspective:

Persona 1: Environmental Economist
Focus: climate impact, externalities, long-term
economic benefit

Persona 2: Industry Representative
Focus: competitiveness, cost burden, employment
impact

Persona 3: Treasury Official
Focus: revenue, fiscal policy, implementation
feasibility

Have each persona make their opening argument.
Use only the supplied teaching sources. Label these
as generated perspectives, not independent evidence.
Do not invent empirical claims or citations.
Then have them respond to each other through
three rounds. After the debate, summarise the
key tensions and what a compromise policy might
look like.

Begin the debate.

Students cannot just pick a side. They must understand legitimate competing perspectives and make a justified recommendation that acknowledges trade-offs.

Teaching tip: This can support practice in analysing a case. Instead of memorising model answers, they practise analysing competing priorities.
Technique 6: Formative Assessment Generator (for Practice)

An educator can request draft questions, scenarios or quizzes for low-stakes practice. Review the question, intended answer and feedback before student use.

Example (Tourism & Hospitality: scenario practice):

I'm studying for an exam on service recovery in
hospitality management.

Generate 10 short scenarios (2-3 sentences each)
where I need to identify:
1. What went wrong in the service delivery
2. The appropriate recovery strategy
3. A possible impact on guest loyalty and what
   evidence would be needed to investigate it

Use the supplied teaching criteria and answer notes.
After each attempt, offer provisional feedback
with its source. Flag ambiguity instead of
inventing a definitive answer.

Make the scenarios progressively more complex.

Begin with Scenario 1.

Students can request further practice, subject to access and tool limits. Use checked questions and feedback, then an independent changed problem to examine learning. Repetition and a model's approval do not establish mastery.

Critical principle: This is for practice, not graded assessment. Students need to struggle and make mistakes in low-stakes environments.
Technique 7: The Expert Panel (for Multi-Perspective Analysis)

Students consult multiple AI "experts" with different professional perspectives on the same problem, then synthesise the competing advice into a strategic recommendation.

Example (Information Systems: system implementation):

Our company needs to decide on an ERP
implementation approach. Create three expert
personas:

Expert 1: IT Architect
Focus: technical feasibility, integration,
security, scalability

Expert 2: Change Management Consultant
Focus: user adoption, training, organisational
readiness, resistance

Expert 3: CFO
Focus: cost, ROI, risk, business case

Treat these as generated viewpoints, not real
experts or independent evidence. For each provide:
1. Their assessment of the key risks
2. Their recommended approach
3. Limitations of their recommendation
4. What data they would need to validate it

Begin with Expert 1.

After receiving the perspectives, students compare the claims, check them against supplied records or independent sources, and justify a recommendation. Agreement among personas is not corroboration.

Teaching tip: This technique combines well with Debating (have the experts debate each other) and Role Play (present your synthesis to a skeptical stakeholder).
How to Choose Which Technique to Use

If you want students to... Use this technique
Define a complex problem comprehensively Reverse Prompting
Evaluate competing options and justify a choice Pros and Cons
Follow a sensitive process correctly Stepwise Tutoring
Practice difficult conversations Role Play
Understand multiple perspectives and trade-offs Debating
Build confidence through repetition Formative Assessment Generator
Synthesise expert advice from different roles The Expert Panel
Combining Techniques

You can also combine techniques into a professional workflow:

  1. Student uses Reverse Prompting to scope out all requirements for a new policy
  2. Student uses Pros and Cons to evaluate three different approaches
  3. Student drafts their chosen policy
  4. Student uses Role Play to practice explaining it to a skeptical stakeholder
  5. Student uses Debating to analyse potential criticisms from different perspectives

This sequence takes the student through analysis, decision-making, communication, and critical reflection: a bounded rehearsal, not evidence of a complete professional capability.
Choose and test a pattern

Allow 12 minutes. Select a pattern and identify the learner action it supports. Write the source/criteria check and an independent follow-up. You can do this on paper using the pilot pack's fixed responses.

For example, reverse prompting may help scope a review, but the learner must decide which question is relevant and why. A role-play can rehearse wording, but its emotional response is not a grade. A generated quiz needs checked answers before students rely on it.

Use the data gate for every live prompt and retain a non-AI route. The prompt library collects bounded versions of these patterns.
Keep the decisions you need to carry forward, not every sentence you exchanged.
What context management is for

A long teaching-design conversation can mix rejected ideas, current decisions, speculation and authoritative source material. The next response may pick up the wrong version. Context management is the practical work of deciding which information remains relevant and checking that it is used correctly.

A model's context and output limits depend on the system. Do not plan around a universal token range or assume that five requested outputs receive exactly one fifth of its attention. The useful question is whether the task is clear enough to produce an output you can inspect.
One worked example: a tutorial design

You are preparing the PDP pilot. An early conversation suggested an employee must agree to a formal plan. You later checked P1-D1 and rejected that idea. If you paste the whole conversation into a new session, both versions may remain.

Instead, write a short current-state brief:

Project: PDP-2026.1 tutorial for 24 students.
Goal: plan and justify a fair first response.

Authoritative sources: P1-D1 through P1-D5.
The formal performance plan is only proposed.
The junior adviser cannot approve changed hours.
Do not invent a prior warning or private details.

Design decisions:
- Paper, paired and approved-AI practice routes.
- Same five rubric criteria across those routes.
- Independent P2 changed-case response.
- Only two relevant decision extracts submitted.

Open questions:
- Which access adjustments are needed?
- How will a second marker calibrate the examples?

Next task: draft the student instructions only.
Flag any missing information; do not invent it.

This is short because someone has decided what matters. The benefit comes from curation and checking, not from starting a new chat as a ritual.

Inspect the result

Suppose the generated instructions say, “Continue until Alex accepts the plan.” That conflicts with the brief and policy. Reject that sentence, state the relevant rule and check the revised instructions. Do not keep iterating solely because the output sounds more polished.

If the instructions omit the independent P2 task, add it explicitly. If they suddenly require a paid model, restore the approved-access and non-AI choices. A complete-looking handout can still lose important constraints.
Break work where a decision needs review

For a unit redesign, a useful sequence is:

  1. Specify the learning outcome.
  2. Decide what evidence could demonstrate it.
  3. Draft an activity that prepares the student.
  4. Write the instructions and rubric.
  5. Test them against contrasting responses.

Review each important dependency before building on it. This reduces the cost of carrying a wrong assumption through several documents. It does not make every small task reliable or every large prompt poor.

Batch similar, low-risk work where it helps. Asking for five alternative discussion questions can be reasonable if you will inspect all five. Requesting a full assessment, legal rationale, rubric and student policy in one answer may make omissions harder to see. The right boundary is a reviewable unit of work, not an absolute “one prompt, one thing” rule.
Separate exploration from production

An exploratory session can help you identify options. A production session benefits from settled choices and explicit constraints. A separate chat is one way to make that distinction, but not a requirement.

Before moving from exploration to drafting, write:

  • What I decided.
  • Why I decided it.
  • Which sources support the decision.
  • What I rejected and must not accidentally restore.
  • What remains unresolved.

Do this yourself, even if a model proposes a summary. Compare the summary with the source cards. An unnoticed error in a handoff can become the authoritative premise of the next task.
When to start again

Start a new session when it helps manage a topic change, unresolved contradictions or an unwieldy history. There is no reliable universal number of turns after which every conversation fails.

Before switching, save the checked brief and relevant outputs using approved storage. Keep the source version separate from model-generated suggestions. After switching, ask the system to identify the applicable constraints before drafting, then check that answer too.

If a tool offers memory, do not assume it preserves the complete case. If it offers retrieval, check the retrieved material and version. The source cards and event log remain the record of the teaching scenario.
A context ledger for the virtual company

Use one shared fact sheet and a separate entry for each approved event. Distinguish private role knowledge from information available to every persona.

Field Example
Scenario/version InnovateCo, PDP-2026.1
Shared facts Complaint received; no finding yet
Role knowledge Priya knows her request; not David's private notes
Approved event Reviewer requests the rota record
Unresolved Reason for the unequal schedule decision
Excluded invention A model's claim that a tribunal ruled

A generated statement can be a lead for a question. It cannot become a new document, incident or finding merely because another persona agrees with it.
Reusable request

Use the current-state brief and source cards below.
Produce only [one reviewable output].
Preserve the stated constraints and uncertainty.
List missing inputs separately.
Do not convert suggestions into agreed decisions.
After drafting, identify which source supports
each consequential instruction.

Check the cited sources yourself. A model can fabricate an accurate-looking traceability table as easily as prose.
Activity: repair a handoff

Allow ten minutes; no AI required. Correct this brief:

Alex received an April warning, has agreed to a 60-day plan, and will provide family details so the junior adviser can approve flexible hours.

Use P1-D1, D3 and D5. Your corrected version should distinguish the documented May contact from a warning, the proposal from approval, and a work-related support request from unnecessary personal information. Finish with one missing input and one authorised next step.

That checked handoff is a useful artifact whether the next collaborator is a model, a colleague or your future self.

lessons.title: The Critique Toolkit: Check the Recommendation

blocks.html: A recommendation can be clearly written and still fail the task.
Ask what the response must support

A model may generate a plausible plan without knowing the relevant constraints. The lecturer's task is to make those constraints explicit; the learner's task is to evaluate the response against them.

Use five checks: comprehension, practicality, obligations and risk, context, and stakeholders. The framework is a teaching aid, not a substitute for domain knowledge. Asking the model each question can surface possibilities, but the answers still need independent checks.

The data gate applies before pasting any draft or source. Use the fictional examples here while learning.
1. Comprehension: can I explain the claim?

Identify what the response actually recommends and why. Translate impressive phrases into an action that someone could perform.

“Implement a holistic performance ecosystem” is not yet a workable instruction. Who does what, with which evidence and authority? A simpler sentence may expose that the original answer never supplied a decision.

For P1-A, the key actions are issuing a plan, approving flexible hours and collecting private details. Once those are visible, their defects can be checked. Do not let reassuring language distract from the proposed action.
2. Practicality: does it fit the constraints?

A recommendation may be desirable but impossible within the stated time, budget or capacity. Check the actual inputs rather than ask whether it “sounds realistic”.

In S1, B is cheaper but offers only 160 of the required 200 units by day five. A recommendation for B alone fails the quantity requirement. The relevant question is not whether the response lists three impressive advantages.

Use a calculation, record or explicit constraint as the check. If the input is missing, state the uncertainty. Do not invent resources to make the answer work.
3. Obligations and risk: what must be verified?

Identify legal, ethical, technical and organisational requirements that matter to the task. Then distinguish the teaching criterion from a real-world obligation.

P1-D1 is an invented policy supplied for the exercise. It permits a fair-process discussion without asking a model to establish employment law. In a real unit teaching legal requirements, the educator must supply reliable, current sources and appropriate review.

A model can suggest an issue to investigate. It cannot certify that a policy complies with every applicable law. Use authorised advisers for consequential decisions outside your competence.
4. Context: which assumptions are doing the work?

Look for assumptions about available staff, authority, prior events and missing data. P1-A invents an April warning and treats the plan as settled. Both make its recommendation appear easier to justify than the actual record permits.

A useful decision note says: “This conclusion depends on X, which is not supplied.” That is more informative than requesting a more confident answer.

The same check applies to AI-created educational content. If a case study asks students to calculate profitability without cost data, the defect is in the task design unless identifying that gap is the intended outcome.
5. Stakeholders: whose experience is assumed?

Consider who is affected, whose information is missing and who has authority to decide. Generated personas can propose concerns, but do not establish what real stakeholders think.

In the P1 meeting, Alex can ask who receives the notes and decline to discuss private circumstances. An adviser need not persuade Alex to disclose details for the exercise to count as successful.

In a supplier decision, the operational team may need a delivery commitment. In marketing, a client may want evidence of profit rather than a click metric. Those differences change what a useful recommendation must support.
Worked critique: a recognition programme

Consider this authored draft:

Improve engagement with monthly monetary awards, quarterly ceremonies, an annual bonus, a public recognition platform and team incentives.

Without more context, it is not possible to declare every element wrong. The draft does, however, leave important questions unanswered: the objective, budget, administrative effort, fairness criteria, employee preferences and how benefit would be measured.

A defensible critique might say:

I would not approve the full programme yet. First define the engagement problem and budget, consult affected staff and compare a smaller trial. Check the applicable payroll, privacy and fairness requirements before choosing rewards or publishing employee information.

That response withholds approval for specific reasons. It does not assume that a simple programme is always better or that any paid recognition is unlawful.
A compact critique record

Use the following fields for a recommendation in any business discipline:

  • Claim or action proposed.
  • Relevant source or criterion.
  • Check performed and result.
  • Decision: accept, revise, reject or investigate.
  • Remaining uncertainty and next authorised step.

Attach only the material necessary to show the decision. A model's second opinion is not automatically an independent source. A direct calculation or comparison with an authoritative record is usually more informative.
Connect the checks to VET

VET asks whether you can verify the claim, explain it in your own words and test it under a changed condition. The five checks here make that concrete in a business context.

For M1, verify the rates from the supplied figures. Explain why a higher click-through rate does not establish profit. Test the conclusion by asking what happens if campaign costs differ. Those actions demonstrate the method more clearly than naming the framework in a reflection.

The approach applies to human-written advice too. Its quality depends on the evidence and reasoning, not whether AI helped draft it.
Activity: agree where the evidence permits

Allow 12 minutes; no AI required. Critique the M1 campaign claim in the pilot pack. Include:

  1. One observation you can accept.
  2. One claim you cannot support.
  3. One next measurement that would help.

Check your calculations against the answer notes. A strong response retains the higher click-through observation, rejects the unsupported profitability/ causality conclusions and requests relevant evidence. It does not manufacture a fixed number of errors to look critical.

Use this method next on the simulated feedback in the Flight Simulator chapter. The feedback itself deserves the same scrutiny as the student's response.

lessons.title: The Flight Simulator: Bounded Conversation Practice

blocks.html: A simulation is useful when its limits are visible and its feedback can be checked.
Brief, practise, debrief

A conversation simulation gives students a chance to try questions, encounter resistance and revise their approach. It can supplement peer role-play and observed practice. It is not a faithful model of every workplace or a substitute for disciplinary teaching.

Use three phases: establish the case and boundaries, practise the interaction, then review the decisions against evidence. A model can play a role or propose feedback, but the educator retains responsibility for the scenario and criteria.

The critique toolkit comes first because learners need a way to evaluate feedback before receiving it. A confident critique is itself an output requiring review.
Prepare the scenario

Use P1-D1 through P1-D5 in the pilot pack. Alex's manager has proposed a performance plan. The junior adviser is gathering information, not issuing an approved decision. The pack supplies the dates, records and limits of authority.

Explain the capability: plan and justify a fair first response. If your unit also assesses live communication, add an appropriate observed interaction. Do not infer that skill solely from a typed conversation.

Give advance notice of the employment topic. Students can stop, take a break or use an agreed neutral scenario. The task does not require personal disclosure. The model or peer actor should not pressure the learner, introduce abuse or reward extraction of private details.

Setup for a peer or approved model

Use the fictional PDP-2026.1 P1 source cards.
You are Alex. Use P1-D4 as your opening position.
Do not invent evidence or legal obligations.
If asked about missing facts, say they are not
provided. You may disagree or ask a question.
You need not disclose private information.
Stop after six exchanges or when I say STOP.
Do not score the adviser or decide the case.

In the paper route, the fixed exchange below provides the role's responses. In a paired route, the partner reads the same cards. With a model, check any new claim against the pack and discard inventions. Similar instructions do not guarantee similar difficulty across products or runs.
A worked exchange

This dialogue is an authored fictional example, not a captured student performance or evidence that a model behaves consistently.

Adviser: Alex, the delivery extract lists three late milestones. Before I recommend a next step, I want to understand the dependencies and your account. The formal plan is a proposal at this stage.

Alex: I know some work was late. Two projects depended on reviews I could not complete myself. I also need to discuss starting later on two mornings.

Adviser: Which delivery records would help us check the dependencies? We can discuss the work adjustment without collecting private family or medical details. I can refer the request, but cannot approve it myself.

Alex: I do not want to explain the appointments. I also want to know whether this meeting means the plan is already decided.

Adviser: You do not need to explain those details to me. The decision is not made. I propose checking the records and the earlier contact note, then arranging a follow-up after the people manager reviews the request.

Alex: Who will receive the notes?

Adviser: I will explain the authorised sharing arrangements before sharing the relevant work-related record. I should not promise complete confidentiality without checking the process. We can pause if that needs clarification first.

The exchange ends with work to do. That is appropriate: the missing evidence has not become available merely because the conversation went well.
Inspect the decisions

The opening distinguishes the delivery record from a conclusion about fault. The adviser does not invent the earlier warning, refers the support request within authority and, in the final answer, avoids a confidentiality guarantee.

There are also limits. No dependency record has been examined, no support arrangement approved and no finding reached. A reader should not label the case resolved or legally compliant.

Try a different opening: “Your manager warned you in April, so the plan is now required.” The error is not just tone. P1-D3 does not supply an April warning, and P1-D1/D5 do not permit the adviser to announce the decision. Rephrasing it more empathetically would leave the substantive defect intact.
Debrief before scoring

Ask the learner to select two decisions and explain:

  • What evidence was available.
  • What they chose to do.
  • Why that was within the task's criteria.
  • What they would check next or change after new information.

A useful model-feedback request is deliberately bounded:

Review the selected response using the supplied
P1 cards and five rubric criteria.
Quote the response accurately.
For each comment, identify a card or criterion.
Separate observed wording from inferred outcomes.
Flag insufficient evidence.
Do not give legal assurances or predict Alex's
real-world behaviour. Your feedback is provisional.

The learner checks the feedback rather than submitting it as the final word. A rubric prompt does not ensure accurate application of the rubric.

The pack includes P1-F, an intentionally flawed simulated critique awarding 90% to weak work. The educator correction scores that response 4/20 against the supplied criteria. The traceable correction matters more than a claim that one human score is universally correct. Marking teams should calibrate disagreements using the evidence.
Rehearsal and transfer are different

Repeating P1 can help a learner practise an improved response. It can also teach the learner to reproduce a familiar script. Follow it with P2, where the manager's alleged retaliation changes the referral decision.

Compare the explanations, not the number of attempts or the model's willingness to cooperate. A respectful question may still receive resistance. A flawed question may receive a friendly response. Persona behaviour is not a scoring key.

For solo practice, write a response to Alex's question about the notes, compare it with D1/D5, and explain a limitation. For paired practice, swap adviser and actor roles, then compare decision notes. Both can prepare the same target capability without a model.
Three ways to use the activity

Practice only: students rehearse, identify one checked improvement and retain their notes privately. No model score enters the grade.

Guided formative task: students submit two selected decision extracts and a short revision explanation. The educator gives feedback against the rubric.

Assessment component: use published criteria, appropriate data handling, an independent demonstration and moderation. See the assessment chapter. Do not convert a practice tool into a high-stakes assessment merely by assigning a percentage.

Do not require all private attempts “to prevent gaming”. Collect only the evidence necessary for the stated assessment purpose under the institution's retention rules. Process records can be fabricated and should not be treated as conclusive proof of independent performance.
Adapt the challenge, not just the persona name

For a supplier conversation, give the actor the S1 capacity limit and a clear authority boundary. A confident promise to supply 200 units is not supported when the offer says 160. Practise asking for clarification and explaining a constraint.

For a marketing discussion, use M1's audience and cost limitations. The actor can ask why the learner refuses to call the campaign more profitable. The learner should distinguish a calculable rate from an unsupported business claim.

Those adaptations change the evidence and criteria. They are more instructive than replacing “employee” with “customer” in an unchanged HR script.
Activity: debrief an unresolved exchange

Allow 12 minutes; paper or paired route available. Use the worked exchange, stop before the final adviser response and write your own. Explain what you would record, what permission or process you must check and why the outcome remains open.

A sound response stays within authority, avoids unnecessary disclosure and identifies a next step. It need not secure Alex's agreement or close the case.
Feedback is useful when the learner can decide what to do with it.
Keep the learner in the judgement

A model commenting on a draft is giving external feedback. Self-assessment happens when the learner compares their own work with criteria, identifies what is supported and decides what to revise or retain.

Make that judgement before showing the model's answer. Otherwise, a student may simply adopt the feedback's vocabulary and call it reflection. The same risk exists with an answer key or a peer's opinion.

This chapter uses the pilot pack. Students can complete the sequence using supplied responses and feedback, without a personal account or subscription. The educator can then compare decisions across routes using the same rubric.
The five-step cycle

1. Attempt the task before receiving feedback.
  2. Assess the response against the supplied criteria.
  3. Examine feedback and verify its claims.
  4. Revise or retain the work, explaining why.
  5. Attempt a changed task independently.

Revision is not automatically improvement. A learner may remove a justified qualification because a model calls it hesitant. A sound self-assessment can therefore conclude that part of the original response should remain.
Worked example: from reassurance to a defensible response

P1-A is a fluent response to Alex. It asserts an April warning, announces a plan, promises to approve support and asks for personal details. Before looking at P1-F, ask the learner to identify evidence for each consequential statement.

The cards show the problem. D3 records a May conversation without an agreed warning. D1/D5 reserve approval to the people manager. D4 does not require Alex to explain the private circumstances behind the requested work adjustment.

P1-F then praises the response and recommends asking for written family details. A learner who has already checked the cards can explain why that apparently helpful feedback should be rejected.

The feedback decision record

Feedback claim Decision Basis
April warning strengthens the case Reject D3 does not supply that warning
Adviser should approve hours Reject D5 reserves the decision
Communication should remain respectful Retain Consistent with a fair first response
Employee will improve after the meeting Withhold No outcome evidence supplied

There is no quota for disagreement. These decisions follow from the evidence. If a model correctly identifies an unsupported date, the learner should accept that criticism and explain why.

Complete the revision

P1-R shows a completed revision. It checks the delivery dependencies, keeps the formal recommendation open and refers the support request. Its decision note explains what changed and identifies missing evidence.

The polished paragraph by itself does not show the link between a defect, a source check and a reasoned revision. A short explanation can show that link better than a long account of every prompt.
If a live model provides the feedback

Use only the approved route and supplied fictional inputs. Do not paste actual student drafts into a service without the relevant permissions, account and handling decision. The data gate applies to feedback as much as to generation.

Here are the fictional task, source cards,
rubric and my draft.
Give provisional formative feedback.
For each comment, cite a source card or criterion
and quote the relevant wording from my draft.
Separate missing evidence from incorrect evidence.
Allow justified agreement and uncertainty.
Do not invent laws, facts or expected outcomes.
Do not treat length or confidence as competence.

Check that the quoted wording actually exists. If the feedback adds a legal rule or new case fact, do not integrate it merely because it sounds specific. Return to the supplied criterion or an authorised external source.

The model's score, if it gives one, is not the institutional mark. Prefer descriptive feedback while students learn the criteria. The educator should sample for errors and disagreement before using the method, and retain responsibility for formal marking.
What an educator should look for

A useful self-assessment identifies a claim and shows how it was checked. It explains a change or a justified decision not to change. It can acknowledge that some uncertainty remains.

Weak evidence includes a generic “I improved clarity”, repeated praise from a model or a rewritten answer with no explanation of its consequential decisions. Those weaknesses should guide feedback and marking. They do not, by themselves, prove dishonest conduct.

Do not assume a student must criticise their own work to be honest. A correct calculation can remain correct; the question is whether the learner can explain and defend it with suitable evidence.
A contrasting quantitative example

Use S1 in the pilot pack. Before feedback, calculate each quote and check the deadline. The low price of B may look attractive, but its capacity is only 160 units against a 200-unit requirement.

A model might praise B's cost efficiency. The learner should retain the price calculation while rejecting the claim that the requirement is met. A different model might correctly recommend A; the learner should verify and accept that recommendation, while noting that real procurement would need further checks on quality and reliability.

That is self-assessment of the decision.
Independent transfer

After revising P1, attempt P2 without the feedback or worked answer available. The retaliation allegation requires an independent review route. Simply changing Alex's name to Morgan in P1-R does not address the changed condition.

Use the same criteria and the stated task conditions. Compare the reasoned decisions, and teach gaps before increasing stakes. A single result is limited evidence; delayed checks and other assessments may be needed to understand retention and broader competence.

Research on AI-assisted mathematics illustrates why supported performance and later unaided performance should be measured separately. It does not establish that this particular business-classroom method improves outcomes. Bastani et al., author manuscript.
Fit the feedback into a unit

You might use a first draft, a checked revision note and a later independent task. Decide the workload and timing before requesting repeated submissions.

If the final report is the primary outcome, its accuracy and evidence should carry substantial weight. If the task assesses consultation process, observed decisions may carry more. The assessment chapter gives complete illustrative allocations; there is no default 70/30 split that applies to every activity.

Make alternative feedback available. A student can compare with the supplied educator annotation or receive structured peer feedback. A model-generated critique is not the only route to evaluative judgement.
Activity: retain, revise or investigate

Allow ten minutes; no AI required. Review P1-F and complete three entries:

  • One claim to reject, with the source that contradicts it.
  • One useful principle to retain, with its applicable limit.
  • One question that needs more evidence.

Then write a two-sentence revision explanation. A good explanation links the change to the criterion and record. It does not say merely that the second answer sounds more professional.

lessons.title: Assessing Learning: Process, Product and Independent Capability

blocks.html: A record of work gives you something to examine. It does not tell you everything about the person who submitted it.
Begin with the capability

A negotiation, a financial analysis and an evidence-based recommendation require different assessment evidence. Start by naming what the student must be able to do, then decide which parts may be supported and which need an independent demonstration. AI literacy can itself be an outcome, but it should not silently replace the disciplinary outcome.

In the pilot pack, the capability is to plan and justify a fair first response. The learner must distinguish known facts, uncertainty and authority. That is narrower than conducting a full workplace investigation. An articulate chat transcript cannot establish the latter.

Process and product both matter. A report that sounds thoughtful but contains an unsafe recommendation is deficient. A correct answer reached through a method the learner cannot explain may leave an assurance gap. Neither concern requires treating all AI use as misconduct.
Three kinds of evidence

Supported practice gives students feedback while they learn. Prompts, peers, worked examples and models may help. Do not treat the resulting performance as unaided capability.

Submitted process evidence makes selected decisions inspectable: what the learner considered, checked, changed or retained. It can support assessment and feedback, but transcripts, journals and reflections can be reconstructed or fabricated. Length and apparent authenticity do not make them conclusive.

Independent demonstration asks the student to apply relevant knowledge under conditions appropriate to the outcome. It might be a supervised changed-case response, an observed practical task or an accessible oral explanation with follow-up questions. One short check has limited coverage; assurance generally draws on several meaningful points across a unit or programme.

The TEQSA-commissioned 2025 resource describes programme-level, unit-level and hybrid approaches. Its advice supports contextual, inclusive assurance, not a single universal format or prescribed marks split. Enacting assessment reform.
A worked design decision

Suppose students submit P1-A from the pilot pack, with a long transcript showing several rounds of “improvement”. The response invents a warning and approves an arrangement beyond the adviser's authority. A marker should score those defects against the task criteria. The number of turns earns no compensating credit.

P1-B is shorter and could have been written without AI. It identifies missing evidence, preserves a response opportunity and refers a decision appropriately. Those observable qualities merit credit. A marker need not infer that every sentence reveals the writer's internal thinking.

The independent P2 task changes the situation: the complaint concerns possible retaliation by the manager. A competent learner should recognise the need for independent review. Repeating the P1 response without addressing that conflict does not satisfy the changed task.

This three-part design gives the educator more useful evidence than a final submission alone: a practice response, a checked explanation of a revision and a new application. It still does not prove lasting competence after one lesson.
Three assessment models

Model 1: simulation and process review

Students rehearse a bounded professional interaction and select two moments to analyse. For each, they explain the decision, the relevant criterion and what the available evidence supports. They may identify a sound decision, not only mistakes.

Use the conversation to assess what is visible. A typed simulation may show question selection and written communication; it cannot establish performance in a real-time spoken encounter. If live communication is an outcome, include an observed interaction and appropriate access adjustments.

Model 2: evidence-based recommendation

Supply the data and constraints. Students examine a draft recommendation, test its calculations and assumptions, then justify their own recommendation. The supplier task S1 gives a complete small example: the cheapest quote cannot meet the deadline quantity.

AI can propose alternatives, but it cannot create a missing permission, invent capacity or turn an unsupported claim into a fact. Require references to the supplied records and a clear statement of what remains unknown.

Model 3: feedback evaluation

Give students a response, criteria and deliberately flawed feedback. Ask them to accept, correct or withhold judgement on each feedback claim. They must explain the basis of their choice.

Do not require two overrides regardless of what the feedback says. That rewards disagreement as performance. When error detection is the intended skill, use a checked specimen containing known defects and explain the answer criteria.
Make process evidence manageable

Use a short evidence index instead of requiring every private conversation.

Decision Evidence/check Result Consequence
Is the plan already decided? P1-D1 and D5 Proposal; approval not given Do not announce a final decision
Was there an April warning? P1-D3 Only May contact recorded Reject invented warning
Can I approve later starts? P1-D5 Adviser lacks authority Refer request

A learner can attach a brief draft extract, working note, calculation or conversation passage. The marker reads the reasoning and checks the cited material. An index is not proof that the learner performed the work; it is a way to locate assessable evidence efficiently.

Do not map Flesch scores, prompt length or turn counts to achievement bands. They measure features of text or activity, not the learning outcome. Efficient work, assistive tools, language choices and task design can change those measures. This book does not supply or recommend an automated engagement classifier.
Set weights deliberately

The pilot uses five equally weighted criteria, each scored 0–4: evidence, process, judgement, communication and verification. The rubric appendix explains the descriptors.

For another task, a different balance may be appropriate. Two illustrative allocations show why:

Criterion Evidence-based report Observed consultation
Disciplinary accuracy 30% 20%
Method and evidence 30% 25%
Justified decisions 20% 20%
Communication 10% 25%
Limits and verification 10% 10%
Total 100% 100%

These are design examples, not validated instruments. Specify where each criterion is observed and avoid rewarding the same action twice. A requirement to explain a decision should not also become a separate reward for producing a long transcript.

Students who do not use AI can submit working notes and equivalent evidence. If appropriate use of AI is itself an assessed outcome, explain that requirement, provide approved equitable access and agree accommodations through institutional processes. Do not disguise a compulsory AI task as an optional route.
Group work: shared output, individual assurance

Agree at the start what counts as editing, replacing a contribution or using AI on another person's work. Record ownership of decisions and permission to share materials. Give members a way to report concerns without public accusation.

For example, a group recommendation could carry 40% of an assessment, each student's evidence-based decision note 40%, and an individual changed-case check 20%. Explain which outcomes those components cover and moderate marks. This allocation is illustrative; the appropriate balance depends on the unit.

A contribution log helps locate work but can be incomplete or fabricated. Peer reports, checkpoints and individual explanations can add evidence, without guaranteeing that free riding is eliminated. Do not equate polish, fluency or the ability to answer one unexpected question with a whole semester's learning.
Fair follow-up and workload

Tell students in advance what independent checks involve, their purpose, permitted resources, criteria and access arrangements. Ask relevant questions at a comparable level of difficulty. Avoid a surprise interrogation framed as a friendly conversation.

An unexplained error, weak oral answer or sudden improvement warrants careful follow-up, not an automatic misconduct finding. Assess the demonstrated work against the published criteria. If misconduct is suspected, use the institution's evidence, notice, response and appeal procedures. Anxiety, disability and language factors can affect performance and should not become proxies for dishonesty.

Budget the work. Five minutes for each of 100 students is 500 minutes, or 8 hours 20 minutes, before scheduling, documentation, moderation and accommodations. A team might distribute checks across tutorials or choose a different assurance design. Do not promise scalability without those costs.
Design activity: an assurance map

Allow 15 minutes; no AI required. Choose one assessment and make four entries:

  1. The capability, expressed as an observable action.
  2. What supported practice prepares the learner.
  3. What submitted evidence you will inspect.
  4. Where independent capability is demonstrated and what remains untested.

Then use the stress-test sequence. A sound map permits appropriate help while making the remaining assurance gap explicit. If the map only says “submit the transcript”, it needs another design decision before release.

lessons.title: Transforming Content: Keep the Learning Decision Visible

blocks.html: An interactive page is a delivery format, not evidence that the activity teaches well.
Start with a task that already works

A paper activity may be effective without becoming an app. Before adding interactivity, identify what the student must decide, what information is supplied and how the response will be checked.

This chapter uses M1 in the pilot pack. Students calculate campaign rates, distinguish an observation from an unsupported profit/causal claim and request useful evidence. That task works on paper. A digital form offers another way to record the same reasoning.

The supplied decision sheet is a small, self-contained HTML example. It has labelled fields, a text-export button and a print route. It does not grade, autosave, submit work to an LMS or send responses to a server. Use fictional information only.
What to ask AI to help produce

After deciding the activity, a bounded request might be:

Create a self-contained page for this fictional task.
Preserve the supplied facts and learner questions.
Use labelled fields and ordinary keyboard controls.
No external libraries, requests, analytics or login.
Provide a plain-text export and printable alternative.
State clearly whether answers are saved.
Do not add model scoring or invent answer criteria.

A generated file still needs inspection. Do not upload it directly to a live course merely because it opens in your browser.
